title: U.S., Korea Should Focus on the Big Picture
text:
U.S., Korea Should Focus on the Big Picture

Newsweek

STAN HONDA/AFP/Getty Images

The following excerpt is from an op-ed published in Newsweek on August 11, 2026, written by Wendy Cutler, Senior Vice President at Asia Society Policy Institute. When I served as the chief U.S. negotiator for the U.S.-Korea Free Trade Agreement (KORUS), I learned that the most durable partnerships are not those without disagreements. They are the ones with enough trust, pragmatism, creativity and shared interest to work through them.KORUS was never an easy negotiation. Sensitive issues, including agriculture, automobiles, and pharmaceuticals tested both sides. Securing U.S. access to Korea’s beef market was among the most sensitive. KORUS succeed in reducing Korea’s steep beef tariffs, while the separate question of when and under what conditions Korea would fully reopen its market remained deeply contentious.After a case of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, commonly called mad cow disease, was discovered in the United States in 2003, Korea and many other partners suspended imports of U.S. beef. When Seoul agreed in 2008 to reopen its market, the decision touched off weeks of mass candlelight demonstrations. Night after night, central Seoul was filled with protesters.At the time, it seemed like the controversy would leave a permanent scar on the bilateral economic relationship. It did not.Read the full op-ed here.
